content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper considers the case of time series forecasting. It argues that in many cases, the time series considered are not stationary. The paper argues that an implication of this is that different prediction models are better or worse over different prediction horizons. The PIs argue that an ensemble model where the weights of the different base learners vary in time can improve the overall performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
+ Mathematically sophisticated treatment of the problem. 

Weaknesses
- The overall justification of the problem is lacking in clarity. It is unclear what type of stationarity the authors are referring to. Strictly stationary time series are rare. Modern time series predictors are expected to handle most non-stationary behaviors by themselves (trends, seasonable behaviors etc)
- It is not clear what the authors exactly mean when they talk to seq2seq models. Do they mean the original, LSTM based seq2seq language translation model? 
- The state of the proposed MDP encompasses the whole history of the data and of all the predictions - making it both huge and of a variable size (growing). The paper does not discuss how they aim to represent this, and perform learning on a space of this size.
- It is not clear what exactly the system learned. For instance, in Figure 3 it is not clear what exactly is on the x axis - is it hours? If yes, the system basically learned that the sun doesn't shine at night-time - however, this is not useful to treat in the form of time varying weights of different predictors - some of them accurate at night, others more accurate at daytime.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: - A significant number of typos exist in the paper which could have been caught by a spellchecker problem. It might indicate a hurried submission.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes an ensemble based approach for forecasting non-stationary time series, where the ensemble weights vary in time. Overall, the paper does not sufficiently justify what type of non-stationarity they are considering and what was exactly learned.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.title: Response to Response Toxy
content.comment:
C1: It is unclear what type of stationarity the authors are referring to.

R1: To avoid confusion, we will further explain the “non-stationarity” in the manuscript.

C2:  It is not clear what the authors exactly mean when they talk to seq2seq models. Do they mean the original, LSTM-based seq2seq language translation model?

R2: We refer Seq2seq models as the one which directly predicts $z_{t+k}$ given $z_{:t}$ for each $k$. This is in contrast to the model with the recursive strategy which predicts the one-step-ahead estimate $z_{t+1}$  given $z_{:t}$, and then iteratively feeds this estimate back as the ground truth to forecast longer horizons. We have further explained these two models in Sections 3.1 and 4.1.1.

C3: The state of the proposed MDP encompasses the whole history of the data and of all the predictions - making it both huge and of variable size (growing). 

R3: As stated in Section 4.1, the state of the proposed MDP does not encompass the whole history of the predictions. It only contains the history of the data and the **current** predictions. Thus, the state of the proposed MDP has a fixed size.

C4: It is not clear what exactly the system learned. 

R4:In Figure 3a, the x-axis represents the prediction timestamps and the unit of the timestamp is hour. The y-axis represents the weights of the 5 base learners. The time-varying weights are consistent with the ranking of the base learners shown in Figure 1a, which shows that the system is able to identify which predators are more accurate at night and which are more accurate at the daytime.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method to dynamically weight an ensemble of time series forecasts. The authors frame the dynamic weighting problem as a Markov decision process and propose utilizing a reinforcement learning algorithm to learn the dynamic weighting through time. In their experiments, their method generally improves the loss metric over each individual forecast.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- Overall method is interesting and the problem of time series forecasting with non-stationary data is very relevant.
- The proposed method is quite simple, still seems somewhat novel, as far as I can tell.

Weakness: 
- I get the feeling that this paper has decided on a lot of arbitrary details and choices without much justification/intuition.
    - First of all, why do the authors believe it was important to frame the dynamic weighting problem as an RL problem? Is the prediction horizon ($H$) fixed, in both training and testing? If so, would it have sufficed to simply done a search over the weightings over time (i.e. search over $M * H$ weight parameters), as a bandit or Bayesian optimization problem?
    - Why did the authors decide to use quantile predictions as the representation of the probabilistic forecasts from the base learners? Have other representations also been investigated (i.e. parameters of a parametric distribution, pdf, cdf)?
    - The reward function makes sense, but there is also little justification: why was it important to have the first term ($R1$) as a regret w.r.t. the best base learner? What are the pitfalls of simply taking the loss of the ensemble forecast? Further, the second term, ($R2$) also seems quite arbitrary: the authors purport that this uniformity term "could potentially reduce error and variance"....is this hypothesis actually supported?
- There are also many details that seem to be missing.
    - For $R2$ term in the reward, how is the "set of near optimal base learners" $M^{*}(S)$ actually determined?
    - For the experiments, how many trials were run to produce the results? 
    - Also in the experiments, for Table 1, what are the numbers reported? How was "a win" determined? With the mean weighted quantile loss? Or the reward?
    - In the same table, how is accuracy measured in the parentheses? With the mean weighted quantile loss? While the quantile loss is a proper score, it would be more intuitive to report other standard metrics of accuracy, e.g. MSE of the median prediction.
    - Do each of the base learners predict the raw time series values or the change in the time series values? If it's the raw values, the orange curve in Figure 3(b) would not be very surprising, especially if the next forecast was simply the previous target value.
- Lastly, it's tough to tell if the proposed method actually achieves a significant improvement over the baselines. E.g., in Table 1, the values for Median and RL-hybrid seem pretty close across all the datasets, but it's impossible to tell if the differences are significant since there are standard errors or confidence bounds reported.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I think the general writing quality and clarity could be improved. For example, there are lots of typos throughout the document (e.g. "quantite", "dependeing", "phenamena", "Winnder"), and some notation seems off (e.g. in Section 4.1.1, at the end of the first paragraph for $\textbf{Direct dynamic}$, we see $w_{i, j}^{m}$....what are $i, j$ indices here?). Also some sentences were just difficult to understand...e.g. 2 lines below equation (5b) "Lastly, we get an ensembled sample for each base learner.."...how is this an ensembled sample? It's a sample from a single base learner, isn't it? Also, in the last paragraph on page 7, under $\textbf{MDP formulation and RL training}$, what is "naive" ensemble dynamics? Overall, the writing doesn't seem very polished, and clarity could benefit from improved writing.
content.summary_of_the_review: While this is an interesting work that tackles a very relevant problem, the presentation could be greatly improved with better justifications, details, presentation of empirical results, and overall writing quality. I look forward to the authors' reponse.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: Response to Reviewer d57d
content.comment:
C1: This paper has made many arbitrary choices without much justification/intuition.

R1: We thank the reviewer for this comment and we have updated the manuscript accordingly to justify our design choices.

* There are two motivations to formulate it as an RL problem: (1) the ensemble weights (action) are sequentially determined, that is, we first make decisions on how to ensemble the time series forecasting results on the first timestamp than the second timestamp and so on, (2) due to the autoregressive dynamics we develop, the ensemble weights (action) will affect the predictions of base learners (state). Due to the feedback of the action on the state, RL is a more suitable formulation.

* The prediction horizon is fixed in both training and testing. Searching for the optimal ensemble strategy by a bandit or Bayesian optimization is doable, but it fails to capture the feedback of ensemble weights on the prediction of the time series base learners.

* Quantile predictions do not require specifying the distribution of the time series output and thus support the distribution-free forecasters.

* By designing the (R1) term as a regret w.r.t. the best base learner, we normalize the reward around zero: If the (R1) term is less than 0, then it means that the ensemble prediction is worse than the single best base learner and the corresponding should be punished. On the other hand, if the (R1) term is greater than 0, then it means that the ensemble prediction is better than the single best base learner and the corresponding should be rewarded. We found that such normalization makes learning more reliable.

* The simple average usually works well if the base learners all have similar performance [1]. We also found that by adding the term (R2), the performance is consistently better than only using the term (R1).

C2: There are also many details that seem to be missing.

R2: We thank the reviewer for this comment and we have updated the manuscript accordingly to further explain the unclear details.

* The “set of near-optimal base learners $M^*(S)$” is determined by the weighted quantile loss of each base learner. Let $m^*$ be the index of the optimal base learners, then  $M^*(S)= \{ m\in M: \mathcal{L}(m) - \mathcal{L}(m^*) <= \epsilon \}$ where $\epsilon>0$ is a threshold.

* For now, we only run the experiments once, we will run the experiments with different random seeds and summarize the statistics errors.
The numbers in Table 1 are the mean weighted quantile loss defined in Equation 7 in the appendix. A “win” method is the one with the smallest mean weight quantile loss on the testing dataset.

* The numbers in the parentheses measure the mean weighted quantile loss of the base learner on the **training** dataset. These numbers show the overfitting of some base learners and explain why our method does not perform very well in such cases.

* The orange curve in Figure 3(b) is the prediction with the raw data (the ground truth data) as the input to the base learners. We only use the prediction results as a reference to show the potential advantage of improving the long-term forecasting accuracy if a more accurate input is available. What is interesting is the green curve which takes the ensemble prediction as the input for the next step predictions. The green curve having a smaller value than the blue curve supports our claim that the auto-regressive ensemble can boost the performance of the base learners.

C3: The general writing quality and clarity could be improved.

R3: We thank the reviewer for pointing out these typos. In particular, we fixed the typos and notations, such as "quantity", "depending", "phenomena", and "Winner". The weights w_{i,j}^m’ is fixed to ‘w_h^m’. In addition, we fixed the typo in  "Lastly, we get an ensembled sample for each base learner..” by  "Lastly, we get a sample for each base learner..” Finally. the ‘direct dynamic’ should be the ‘naive dynamic’. 

[1] Jeremy Smith and Kenneth F Wallis. A simple explanation of the forecast combination puzzle. Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics, 71(3):331–355, 2009

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper discusses the problem of forecasting using time series datasets by introducing a Markov Decision Process within a developed framework (TS GYM), which succeeds in addressing three obstacles met in this task: (1) the assumption of time invariant techniques with reference to the future control intervals, (2) the lack of adaptation to the initial point, (3) the non deployment of base learning methods. The suggested predictions are performed with a pipeline using deep Reinforcement Learning dynamically by successively inputting a currently optimal sample to every base learning algorithm.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
S1: The framework is developed from scratch and seems creative.
S2: The authors mention the existing traditional static ensemble algorithms and underline the novelty of their system in increasing the predictive accuracy. 

W1: Tables 1 and 2 seem confusing to me: what are the metrics reported in them? The paper supports that the table contains: ''three metrics, winning rate, average ranking, and averaged stability score'. Are they all reported in this table in each column (each column I guess refers to each of the datasets)", but this is not exactly described there. 

W2: The achieved metrics do not seem 'winning' in all cases. Even when they are, the seem to be marginally better the competing metrics (how is the statistical error excluded?). It is not clear what the bold ones report.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: the paper is ok written, but the tables seem confusing: where are the three metrics mentioned in text (winning rate, average ranking, and averaged stability score). The metrics are crucial for this paper, because they seem to prove the superiority of the model; yet they are not clear from the tables.

Quality: the experiments demonstrate the efficiency of dynamic ensemble system. Pipeline is tested on real world datasets. However the achieved metrics do not seem 'winning' in all cases. Even when they are, the seem to be marginally better the competing metrics (how is the statistical error excluded?).

Novelty: the system is compared to the previous ensemble algorithms and demonstrates innovation. However, the authors should make sure that the metrics they report are indeed better than the literature's ones. This is not obvious from the tables reported here.

Reproducibility: I didn't find a link to the system implementation.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall an ok paper with some weaknesses; presentation can be improved especially in the quantitative parts and can be more supported by a legend/explanation.

content.title: Response to Reviewer oHSn
content.comment:
C1: What are the metrics reported in Tables 1 and 2? What are “three metrics, winning rate, average ranking, and averaged stability score”?

R1: The metrics reported in Tables 1 and 2 are the mean weighted quantile loss defined in Equation 7 in the appendix.

The metrics “winning rate, average ranking, and averaged stability score'” are measured based on the results of mean weighted quantile loss. In particular,

* winning rate measures the percentage of datasets that one method wins
* average ranking measures the rank of one method among all methods averaged over all datasets
* averaged stability score measures the amount of \% degradation compared with winning method

We have revised the draft accordingly to make these metrics clear.

C2: The achieved metrics seem to be marginally better than the competing metrics.

R2: The main reason that the proposed method does not perform well is the overfitting of the time series base learners. It is not that our method fails to capture the performance patterns of the base learners but that overfitting base learners confuse the agent.
We will retrain the base learners to avoid overfitting and adding statistical errors. 

C3: The tables seem confusing: where are the three metrics mentioned in text.

R3: We have added that the results in Table 1 are measured by the mean weighted quantile loss.

C4: The achieved metrics do not seem 'winning' in all cases and the achieved metrics seem to be marginally better than the competing metrics.

R4:: We will fix the overfitting issue of the base learners and improve the metrics or our method accordingly. The experiments with different random seeds will be run to summarize the statistics errors.

Best wishes,
Authors of Paper3677
